question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ |A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}. \]

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

\begin{align*} |A| &= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 6 & -3 \\ -12 & - 2 & 0\\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot (-1)^{3+1} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ - 2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=1 \cdot (-6) \\[5pt] &=-6 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain

\[ |A^{-1}|=\dfrac{1}{|A|}=-\dfrac{1}{6}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

\[ \det(M N) = \det(M) \cdot \det(N). \]

In our case, this gives

\[ \det(K) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1 & -7 \\ 4 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \det \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 8\\ 0 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

  • For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

  • For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(K) &= \begin{vmatrix} 5 & \color{blue}0 & 2 \\ -3 &\color{blue} 1 & -7 \\ 4 & \color{blue}0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 8\\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}-3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 5& 2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \cdot (-3)(-1)^{3+3} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] &=(15-8)\cdot (-3)(8-9) \\[5pt] &= 7\cdot 3\\[5pt] &=21. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of a Product

question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ |A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}. \]

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

\begin{align*} |A| &= \begin{vmatrix} 4 & -2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3 &2\\ -3 & 5 &6 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=-1(-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} -2 & -4 \\ 5 & 6 \end{vmatrix}+ 3(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ -3 & 6 \end{vmatrix}+ 2(-1)^{2+3} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-12+20)+3(24-12)-2(20-6) \\[2pt] &= 8+36-28 \\[5pt] &= 16 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain

\[ |A^{-1}|=\dfrac{1}{|A|}=\dfrac{1}{16}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{red}144}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}158}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}102}+{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{red}144}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}158}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}102}+{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{}144} & {\color{}158} & {\color{}102} \end{vmatrix} . \end{align*}

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \\ {\color{red}144} & {\color{red}158} & {\color{red}102} \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -7 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \end{vmatrix} &= 0 +1(-1)^{2+3} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 144 & 158 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] & = -(2\cdot 158-4\cdot 144) \\[2pt] &= -(316-576)\\[5pt] &= 260 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant

question.text: Given that $ \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ a & b+2 \end{vmatrix} = 8 $, find $ \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b \end{vmatrix} .$
question.explanation:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ a+3 & b \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ {\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}3} & {\color{red}(b+2)}-{\color{blue}2} \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ {\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}3} & {\color{red}(b+2)}-{\color{blue}2} \end{vmatrix} &= \underbrace{ \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ {\color{red}a} & {\color{red}b+2} \end{vmatrix} }_{\large 8} + \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}-2} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 8+(-6+6) \\[5pt] &= 8. \end{align*}
